desc:
You are given a binary string s. Call a substring dominant if the number of ones in it is at least the square of the number of zeros in it. A substring with no zeros is therefore always dominant.

Return how many substrings of s are dominant. Substrings are counted by position, so equal substrings at different places count separately.

For example, s = "00011" gives 5 (the substrings 1, 1, 11, 01 and 011), and s = "101101" gives 16.
constraints: s contains only the characters '0' and '1'
hints: Checking all O(n<sup>2</sup>) substrings with prefix sums is fine for small n. For bigger n, find something that limits the interesting cases.
If a substring has z zeros it needs at least z2 ones, so its length is at least z + z2. Hence z can be at most about sqrt(n).

Fix the left end l and the number of zeros z ≤ sqrt(n). The right ends with exactly z zeros form a contiguous range (between two consecutive zero positions). Inside that range the condition becomes a lower bound on the length, so you can count the valid right ends with arithmetic.
editorial: Let z and o be the zeros and ones of a substring; it is dominant if o ≥ z2, i.e. if its length L = z + o satisfies L ≥ z2 + z. Since L ≤ n, only substrings with z up to about sqrt(n) (roughly 63 for n = 4000) can qualify.

Collect the positions of the zeros in a list Z. For a left end l let zi be the number of zeros before l. The right ends r that give exactly z zeros lie in the interval [a, b], where a = l if z = 0 and a = Z[zi + z - 1] otherwise, and b = Z[zi + z] - 1 (or n - 1 if there is no such zero). Inside that interval the number of zeros is fixed, so the condition is simply r - l + 1 ≥ z2 + z, i.e. r ≥ l + z2 + z - 1. The number of valid right ends is the size of [max(a, l + z2 + z - 1), b] if it is non-empty.
Looping over every l and every z with z2 + z ≤ n - l costs O(n · sqrt(n)) with O(1) work per pair. This is far better than O(n2) and about 234,000 steps for n = 5000.
